stops.note: a step, a pace, from the Proto-Indo-European root pete- (to spread)

stops.meaning: to step, to walk, to pass

stops.note: carried into French as the basic verb for 'to pass'
literally 'not passable', formed from in- (not) and passe (a passing); said to have been introduced by Voltaire as a polite alternative to cul-de-sac
stops.meaning: an impassable road, a dead end

stops.note: Voltaire is credited with using it in French for a dead-end street
stops.meaning: a situation with no clear way forward

current_meaning: a situation in which no progress can be made; a deadlock
